LESSON 72 OF 106·Social Engineering and the Human Factor

Phishing: Anatomy of a Message

Read a suspicious message from the outside in — channel, identity, request and context — with the indicators, the layers to check, and the design of a targeted message.

Foundation15 min
Why this matters

A phishing message is a request delivered by a channel you already trust. Learning to read one properly is more useful than learning to spot a bad link, because the link is the part that changes.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • The message establishes a plausible context first, so the request feels like a continuation of something already in progress.
  • A call to action is the point of the message, and everything else exists to make the action seem ordinary.
  • The sender identity is the easiest thing to fake, and the display name in particular proves nothing.
  • A link visible text and its real destination are independent, which is why hovering and reading is a real check.
  • A message that creates urgency or fear reduces the reader willingness to verify, which is the whole objective.

The background

  • Bulk phishing produced a huge volume of obviously bad messages, which trained people to be sceptical at a low threshold.
  • Spear phishing reduced volume and improved personalisation, which reset that threshold in attackers favour.
  • Business email compromise refined the approach further by removing any technical trick at all.
  • Email authentication standards reduced spoofing of the domain, which pushed attackers toward impersonating a real colleague instead.

Real-world examples

  • A message from a real colleague compromised account is technically perfect, so header and domain checks find nothing.
  • A password reset prompt that leads to a lookalike domain defeats a user who only checks that the page looks right.
  • An attachment in a thread the user started, replying to something they actually sent, defeats careful inspection of the thread.

What to look for

  • Check the actual sender address and reply-to, not the display name.
  • Check where the link goes before clicking, and prefer navigating to a known address instead.
  • Check whether the request is urgent, unusual, or bypasses a process you normally follow.
  • Check whether the message expects you to reveal a credential, a code, or payment details.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Recognize and Report Phishing

Working through an official list of the common signs of a phishing message, and the recognise-resist-report structure that goes with them

Open CISA resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Teach people to hover and read the destination, and to type known addresses rather than follow links.
  • Require multi-factor authentication so a successful phishing attempt does not mean account access.
  • Use a separate mailbox for external mail and payment requests, so the ordinary inbox is not the place where trust is tested.
  • Add a banner marking external or unverified senders, and expect people to read it.
  • Make reporting a single click, and monitor the report rate as a real security metric.
